Welcome back. Everything on this page runs real R in your browser — same setup as the other coding activities. Before you run **Welch's *t*-test**, you inspect your data: fix clear errors, look at shape and extremes, and decide whether a transform helps. You will **not** run the test itself.

The first time you click **Run Code**, your browser downloads R once (a few seconds). After that it is quick.

This roadmap is for **Welch's *t*-test** — comparing two **independent** groups when you do **not** assume equal variances (`t.test(..., var.equal = FALSE)` in R). One-sample, paired, Student's equal-variance, linear regression, and ANOVA need different checks — do not use this flowchart for those tests.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  load[Load and inspect data] --> step1["Step 1: remove impossible values, keep missing"]
  step1 --> naRm["Summaries use na.rm = TRUE"]
  naRm --> step2["Step 2: flag IQR outliers — do not remove yet"]
  step2 --> step3["Step 3: histogram + Shapiro-Wilk"]
  step3 --> transform{Transform needed?}
  transform -->|yes| recheck[Repeat histogram + Shapiro on new scale]
  transform -->|no| step4
  recheck --> step4["Step 4: re-flag outliers on analysis scale"]
  step4 --> decide[Decide whether to remove flagged points]
  decide --> ttest["Run Welch's t-test — not in this activity"]
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What this checklist does — and does not do

This workflow helps you **explore** data before a parametric test — it does not certify that Welch's *t*-test is valid.

- **Shapiro-Wilk:** A small p-value means "looks non-normal in this sample," not "you must abandon Welch's *t*-test." A large p-value is **not** proof of normality. With moderate *n* per group, Welch's *t*-test is often robust to mild skew.
- **IQR fences:** Flag points for review — they are not necessarily errors. The fence is an exploratory rule, not a formal test.
- **Transforms:** If you log-transform and then run Welch's *t*-test, you are testing a **different hypothesis** on a different scale. That can be fine — but say so in your write-up.
- **Other Welch's *t*-test assumptions:** Independence comes from study design (no paired or repeated measures). You do **not** need equal variances between groups — that is why you use Welch. Check approximate normality in **each group** (histogram + Shapiro per group, or on the scale you will analyze).
:::

## 4. Step 1 — missing and impossible values *(Coding Assignment 3, Q4)*

Two different data problems show up in real datasets: **missing** values (`NA`) and **impossible** values (e.g. negative counts or bill depths). They need different handling.

- **Missing** means no measurement was recorded — keep those rows for now.
- **Impossible** means a sign error or bad entry — remove those rows.

Use `filter(is.na(bill_depth_mm) | bill_depth_mm >= 0)` to drop impossible depths while keeping missing ones. After this step, every numeric summary uses **`na.rm = TRUE`** so R skips the remaining `NA`s.

**Step 1 — trim impossible values.** Bill depth cannot be negative. Remove rows where `bill_depth_mm` is negative. **Keep** rows where `bill_depth_mm` is missing. Save the result as `penguin_clean`.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## `|` means "or"

Inside `filter()`, the vertical bar **`|`** means **"or"**. The condition `is.na(bill_depth_mm) | bill_depth_mm >= 0` keeps a row if **either** the depth is missing **or** it is zero or positive.

Writing `filter(bill_depth_mm >= 0)` alone silently **drops the missing rows** — because `NA >= 0` evaluates to `NA`, not `TRUE`.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| exercise: trim_impossible
penguin_clean <- penguin_data |>
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="trim_impossible"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?filter`: keep rows where conditions are TRUE.

```r
mtcars |>
  filter(is.na(mpg) | mpg >= 0)
```

Keep missing bill depths **or** non-negative depths.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="trim_impossible"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
penguin_clean <- penguin_data |>
  filter(is.na(bill_depth_mm) | bill_depth_mm >= 0)
```

50 rows — no negative values in this dataset, so nothing was removed. The one missing measurement is still there. **Confirming there are no impossible values is itself a reportable result.**
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| exercise: trim_impossible
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "
")
if (!exists("penguin_clean", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Save the filtered table as `penguin_clean`."
  )
} else {
  bc <- get("penguin_clean", envir = .envir_result)
  n <- nrow(bc)
  n_na <- sum(is.na(bc$bill_depth_mm))
  n_neg <- sum(!is.na(bc$bill_depth_mm) & bc$bill_depth_mm < 0)
  used_or <- grepl("is\.na\s*\(\s*bill_depth_mm\s*\)", code) && grepl("\|", code)
  if (n == 50 && n_na == 1 && n_neg == 0) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "50 rows — no negatives found, missing value kept. That is the correct outcome here."
    )
  } else if (n == 49 && n_na == 0) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "error",
      message = "`filter(bill_depth_mm >= 0)` alone drops missing rows. Use `is.na(bill_depth_mm) | bill_depth_mm >= 0`."
    )
  } else if (!used_or) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Use `filter(is.na(bill_depth_mm) | bill_depth_mm >= 0)` so missing rows stay."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Filter with `is.na(bill_depth_mm) | bill_depth_mm >= 0` and save as `penguin_clean`."
    )
  }
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: check_missing
```

## 5. Flag distributional outliers *(Coding Assignment 3, Q5)*

**Step 2 — flag outliers.** Using only the non-missing bill depths in `penguin_clean`, calculate the upper fence of the 1.5 × IQR rule: Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Save it as `upper_fence` and print it. Also count how many non-missing bill depths exceed that fence and save the count as `n_raw_outliers`. Print both values. Do not remove any rows.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The 1.5 × IQR rule is a **screening tool**. Points above the fence deserve a look; they are not automatically errors.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| setup: true
#| exercise: upper_fence
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Adelie", year == 2007)
penguin_clean <- penguin_data |>
  filter(is.na(bill_depth_mm) | bill_depth_mm >= 0)
```

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| exercise: upper_fence
upper_fence <- 
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="upper_fence"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

From `?quantile`: `quantile(x, probs, na.rm = FALSE)`. From `?IQR`: `IQR(x, na.rm = FALSE)`.

```r
q3 <- quantile(mtcars$mpg, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
fence <- q3 + 1.5 * IQR(mtcars$mpg, na.rm = TRUE)
n_out <- sum(mtcars$mpg > fence, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Use the 75th percentile and IQR of non-missing bill depths, then count values above the fence.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="upper_fence"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
upper_fence <- quantile(penguin_clean$bill_depth_mm, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  1.5 * IQR(penguin_clean$bill_depth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
n_raw_outliers <- sum(penguin_clean$bill_depth_mm > upper_fence, na.rm = TRUE)
upper_fence
n_raw_outliers
```

The upper fence is about 21.4 mm — one penguin has a bill depth above it.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| exercise: upper_fence
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!exists("upper_fence", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Save the result as `upper_fence`."
  )
} else {
  uf <- as.numeric(get("upper_fence", envir = .envir_result))
  has_q <- grepl("quantile\\s*\\(", code)
  has_iqr <- grepl("IQR\\s*\\(", code)
  has_count <- grepl("n_raw_outliers", code) && grepl("sum\\s*\\(", code)
  n_out <- if (exists("n_raw_outliers", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
    get("n_raw_outliers", envir = .envir_result)
  } else NA
  if (length(uf) == 1 && abs(uf - 21.4) < 0.5 && has_q && has_iqr && !is.na(n_out) && n_out == 1) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "Upper fence ≈ 21.4 mm. One bill depth sits above it — flag it, do not delete it yet."
    )
  } else if (has_q && has_iqr && !is.na(n_out) && n_out == 1) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = paste0("Upper fence ≈ ", round(uf, 1), " mm with ", n_out, " outlier. Good.")
    )
  } else if (!has_count) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Also count outliers: `n_raw_outliers <- sum(penguin_clean$bill_depth_mm > upper_fence, na.rm = TRUE)`."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Use `quantile(..., 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) + 1.5 * IQR(..., na.rm = TRUE)` and count values above the fence."
    )
  }
}
```

## 7. Shapiro-Wilk on the raw scale *(Coding Assignment 3, Q7)*

Run `shapiro.test()` on the non-missing bill depths in `penguin_clean`. Save the result as `shapiro_raw` and print it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Reading Shapiro-Wilk output

The null hypothesis is **normality**. A **small p-value** (conventionally below 0.05) means the data look **inconsistent with** a normal distribution. A **large p-value** means you do **not** have evidence against normality — not proof that the data are perfectly normal.

**Do not treat p > 0.05 as a green light or p < 0.05 as an automatic veto** — combine this test with your histogram and sample size.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| exercise: shapiro_raw
shapiro_raw <- 
  
```

::: {.hint exercise="shapiro_raw"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Pass the bill-depth vector directly.

```r
shapiro.test(mtcars$mpg)
```

Use non-missing values from `penguin_clean$bill_depth_mm`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="shapiro_raw"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
shapiro_raw <- shapiro.test(penguin_clean$bill_depth_mm)
shapiro_raw
```

p ≈ 0.029 — evidence against normality on the raw scale.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| exercise: shapiro_raw
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("shapiro\\.test\\s*\\(", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Call `shapiro.test()` on bill depths."
  )
} else if (!exists("shapiro_raw", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Save the result as `shapiro_raw`."
  )
} else {
  sr <- get("shapiro_raw", envir = .envir_result)
  if (!is.null(sr$p.value) && sr$p.value < 0.05) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = paste0("p = ", signif(sr$p.value, 3), " — raw bill depths fail the normality check.")
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Run `shapiro_raw <- shapiro.test(penguin_clean$bill_depth_mm)` on non-missing values."
    )
  }
}
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
In the same birds, bill *length* would pass Shapiro-Wilk — so a failing depth distribution is specific to this variable, not the whole dataset.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why did square root fail here?

Square root is the standard transform for **right-skewed counts** — parasite loads, cell counts, tick burdens. **Bill depth is a continuous measurement**, not a count. It improved the Shapiro-Wilk p-value but not enough to pass 0.05. When square root is not enough for a right-skewed continuous variable, a **log** transform is the next thing to try.

On **Coding Assignment 3**, worm counts **are** counts, and square root is the right first transform there. Do not mechanically apply log to that assignment.
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: assumptions_lab
#| exercise: upper_fence_log
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!exists("upper_fence_log", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Save the result as `upper_fence_log`."
  )
} else {
  ufl <- as.numeric(get("upper_fence_log", envir = .envir_result))
  has_q <- grepl("quantile\\s*\\(", code)
  has_iqr <- grepl("IQR\\s*\\(", code)
  has_count <- grepl("n_log_outliers", code) && grepl("sum\\s*\\(", code)
  n_out <- if (exists("n_log_outliers", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
    get("n_log_outliers", envir = .envir_result)
  } else NA
  if (length(ufl) == 1 && abs(ufl - 3.073) < 0.05 && has_q && has_iqr && !is.na(n_out) && n_out == 0) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "Zero log-scale outliers — the transform pulled the raw outlier inside the fence."
    )
  } else if (has_q && has_iqr && !is.na(n_out) && n_out == 0) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = paste0("Upper log fence ≈ ", round(ufl, 3), " with ", n_out, " outliers. Good.")
    )
  } else if (has_q && has_iqr && !is.na(n_out) && n_out == 1) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Re-check your count — after the log transform, zero values should exceed the fence."
    )
  } else if (!has_count) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Also count outliers: `n_log_outliers <- sum(penguin_transformed$log_depth > upper_fence_log, na.rm = TRUE)`."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Apply the IQR fence formula to `log_depth` and count values above it."
    )
  }
}
```

## 18. Impossible vs. extreme *(Coding Assignment 3, Q14)*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why keep the deep bill?

One Adelie penguin had a bill depth of **21.5 mm** — above the raw-scale IQR fence. That value is **extreme but biologically plausible**. Large-billed individuals occur in wild populations. It is not a data-entry error the way a **negative** depth would be.

The log transformation **compressed the right tail** of the skewed raw depths, making the distribution much more symmetric, bringing the Shapiro-Wilk test in line with the normality assumption, and pulling that bird inside the transformed-scale fence — without throwing away real observations. Passing Shapiro-Wilk after a transform does not mean the original data were "fixed" — you changed the scale.

On **Coding Assignment 3** you will explain this same distinction in prose for worm counts in deer mice.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Try this with a partner.** One of you explains why negative counts get removed but high counts stay; the other explains why log worked here but square root did not. Swap roles.
:::

## 19. Recap — verbs you practiced

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does each function do?

| Function | Role |
|----------|------|
| `library(tidyverse)` | Loads dplyr, ggplot2, and related packages |
| `library(palmerpenguins)` | Loads the `penguins` dataset |
| `filter()` | Keeps rows matching a condition (`species == "Adelie"`, `is.na(...) \| ... >= 0`) |
| `mutate()` | Adds transformed columns (`sqrt_depth`, `log_depth`) |
| `glimpse()` | Quick look at rows, columns, and types |
| `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Average of a numeric column, skipping missing values |
| `quantile(..., 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)` | 75th percentile for the IQR fence |
| `IQR(..., na.rm = TRUE)` | Interquartile range for the 1.5×IQR rule |
| `sum(x > fence, na.rm = TRUE)` | Counts values above an outlier fence |
| `ggplot()` + `geom_histogram()` | Visual check of distribution shape |
| `shapiro.test()` | Formal test of normality (H₀: data are normal) |
| `sqrt()` | Square-root transformation (for right-skewed **counts**) |
| `log()` | Natural-log transformation (when sqrt is not enough for right-skewed data) |

If you can explain each row in your own words, you have covered the core of **Coding Assignment 3**.
:::

```{webr}
library(palmerpenguins)
gentoo <- penguins |> filter(species == "Gentoo")
shapiro.test(gentoo$flipper_length_mm)
shapiro.test(sqrt(gentoo$flipper_length_mm))
shapiro.test(log(gentoo$flipper_length_mm))
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
All three p-values stay below 0.05. Flipper length spans only 203–231 mm, so no monotonic transform can fix this distribution. The honest next step is a **nonparametric test** (e.g. **Mann-Whitney** for two independent groups) — not another transform.
:::
